analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers refinance student loans at lower fixed rates, eases repayment, and makes student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill was never considered by any committee and died at the end of the 115th Congress in January 2019, without a single cosponsor or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let people with older federal or private student loans refinance into fixed-rate federal loans at lower 2016-era rates, and would let private student loan borrowers move into federal loans if they are current on payments. It would also restore subsidized loans for graduate students, simplify repayment into a choice between a standard 10-year plan and an income-based plan, automatically enroll delinquent borrowers in affordable plans, expand loan forgiveness to adjunct faculty, and delete the special rule that makes student loans nearly impossible to wipe out in bankruptcy.
analysis.who_benefits: People still repaying student loans — especially borrowers with older federal loans carrying higher interest rates and borrowers with high-interest private loans. They could refinance at fixed rates of roughly 3.8% to 6.3% (the 2016-17 federal rates), enroll in simpler income-based repayment with a $0 option for low earners, have interest capped at 50% of principal, get forgiveness after 20 years instead of 25, and — if genuinely unable to pay — discharge the debt in bankruptcy like other debt. Adjunct and part-time faculty would gain access to public service loan forgiveness. Graduate students would regain subsidized loans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers with older or private loans

how_it_helps.text: Borrowers could refinance federal and old FFEL loans into new federal loans at the fixed interest rates in effect for 2016-17, which were lower than the rates many older loans carry.

Borrowers with private student loans who are current on payments could transfer them into federal loans at fixed federal rates, with eligibility rules aimed at borrowers with the greatest financial need.
It would remove the special bankruptcy rule protecting student loans, letting borrowers discharge them like almost any other debt.
It would reinstate subsidized Stafford Loans for graduate students, so interest would not pile up while they are in school.

It would cap interest accrual during repayment at 50% of the original principal, set $0 payments for low-income borrowers, shorten loan forgiveness to 20 years of payments, and automatically enroll borrowers who are 120 days delinquent into the income-driven plan with the lowest payment.
Part-time and adjunct faculty would become eligible for public service loan forgiveness, and payments made on refinanced loans would count toward existing forgiveness timelines.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and taxpayers, who would absorb the cost of refinancing older loans at lower fixed rates, cover $0 payments and interest subsidies for low-income borrowers, and lose repayment claims when loans are discharged in bankruptcy. Private student lenders would also lose borrowers and future interest income, since the government would pay off their loans in full.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; private student lenders lose business

drawbacks.text: Refinancing old federal and private loans at 2016-era rates would cost the federal government money: borrowers would pay less interest than they currently owe, and private lenders would be paid off in full while taxpayers take over the loans.

Making student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy could raise borrowing costs or lead lenders to restrict credit, since loans could no longer be collected from borrowers who declare bankruptcy — a common objection to such proposals.

The bill would eliminate most existing repayment plan options, leaving borrowers only a 10-year standard plan and one income-based plan, which some borrowers on graduated or extended plans would experience as a loss of choice.

The bill would allow the IRS to share taxpayer return information with the Department of Education for automatic enrollment and income recertification in income-driven repayment — an expansion of tax data sharing, albeit with use restrictions and an opt-out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to borrowers are substantial and concrete — lower fixed interest rates, bankruptcy relief, simpler repayment — but the costs are real: the federal government would bear the difference between old high rates and the refinanced rates, plus losses when loans are discharged in bankruptcy, and the bill text does not say how those costs would be funded. Congress ended before any committee even weighed the design, so no cost analysis was ever produced.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees, then to a subcommittee, and no committee ever voted on it before the two-year congressional term ended, so it died without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the HIGHER ED Act on April 18, 2018.
It was referred to three House committees — Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, and Ways and Means — meaning each could have considered the parts within its jurisdiction.
On May 22, 2018, the Judiciary portion was referred to its Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed.
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor in the House.
The 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders, federal loan servicers, and the collection industry are better off: the borrowers they might have lost to refinancing, automatic enrollment, or bankruptcy discharge remain their customers. Borrowers with older, higher-rate loans keep paying their current rates.

for.name: Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee and its Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to a subcommittee on May 22, 2018, where it remained without action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Private student loan lenders and student loan servicing companies
against.what_they_did: Have consistently opposed student-loan refinancing and bankruptcy-discharge legislation that would move loans to the federal government or wipe out private loan debt.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for a partisan vote; a Democratic sponsor introduced it with no Republican or Democratic cosponsors, and it died in committee without any recorded position by either party.

industries.industry: Private student lenders (e.g., Sallie Mae and similar lenders)
industries.note: Borrowers in good standing could move their private loans into fixed-rate federal loans, draining lenders' most creditworthy borrowers, and private student loans would lose their special bankruptcy protection. The bill also required lenders to report default and delinquency data to regulators.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: Automatic enrollment into income-driven repayment for delinquent borrowers, automatic income recertification, and simpler plan menus would reduce the volume of defaulted accounts routed through collection. Fewer borrowers in hardship tracks means less fee and collection revenue.
Taxpayers would bear the cost of refinancing older high-rate loans at lower rates and of loans discharged in bankruptcy, while gaining from fewer defaults and a simpler repayment system.
